2: name: debug-buttercup
3: description: >
4:   Debugs the Buttercup CRS (Cyber Reasoning System) running on Kubernetes.
5:   Use when diagnosing pod crashes, restart loops, Redis failures, resource pressure,
6:   disk saturation, DinD issues, or any service misbehavior in the crs namespace.
7:   Covers triage, log analysis, queue inspection, and common failure patterns
8:   for: redis, fuzzer-bot, coverage-bot, seed-gen, patcher, build-bot, scheduler,
9:   task-server, task-downloader, program-model, litellm, dind, tracer-bot,
10:   merger-bot, competition-api, pov-reproducer, scratch-cleaner, registry-cache,
11:   image-preloader, ui.
12: ---
13: 
14: # Debug Buttercup
15: 
16: ## When to Use
17: 
18: - Pods in the `crs` namespace are in CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, or restarting
19: - Multiple services restart simultaneously (cascade failure)
20: - Redis is unresponsive or showing AOF warnings
21: - Queues are growing but tasks are not progressing
22: - Nodes show DiskPressure, MemoryPressure, or PID pressure
23: - Build-bot cannot reach the Docker daemon (DinD failures)
24: - Scheduler is stuck and not advancing task state
25: - Health check probes are failing unexpectedly
26: - Deployed Helm values don't match actual pod configuration
27: 
28: ## When NOT to Use
29: 
30: - Deploying or upgrading Buttercup (use Helm and deployment guides)
31: - Debugging issues outside the `crs` Kubernetes namespace
32: - Performance tuning that doesn't involve a failure symptom
33: 
34: ## Namespace and Services
35: 
36: All pods run in namespace `crs`. Key services:
37: 
38: | Layer | Services |
39: |-------|----------|
40: | Infra | redis, dind, litellm, registry-cache |
41: | Orchestration | scheduler, task-server, task-downloader, scratch-cleaner |
42: | Fuzzing | build-bot, fuzzer-bot, coverage-bot, tracer-bot, merger-bot |
43: | Analysis | patcher, seed-gen, program-model, pov-reproducer |
44: | Interface | competition-api, ui |
45: 
46: ## Triage Workflow
47: 
48: Always start with triage. Run these three commands first:
49: 
50: ```bash
51: # 1. Pod status - look for restarts, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled
52: kubectl get pods -n crs -o wide
53: 
54: # 2. Events - the timeline of what went wrong
55: kubectl get events -n crs --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
56: 
57: # 3. Warnings only - filter the noise
58: kubectl get events -n crs --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
59: ```
60: 
61: Then narrow down:
62: 
63: ```bash
64: # Why did a specific pod restart? Check Last State Reason (OOMKilled, Error, Completed)
65: kubectl describe pod -n crs <pod-name> | grep -A8 'Last State:'
66: 
67: # Check actual resource limits vs intended
68: kubectl get pod -n crs <pod-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
69: 
70: # Crashed container's logs (--previous = the container that died)
71: kubectl logs -n crs <pod-name> --previous --tail=200
72: 
73: # Current logs
74: kubectl logs -n crs <pod-name> --tail=200
75: ```
76: 
77: ### Historical vs Ongoing Issues
78: 
79: High restart counts don't necessarily mean an issue is ongoing -- restarts accumulate over a pod's lifetime. Always distinguish:
80: - `--tail` shows the end of the log buffer, which may contain old messages. Use `--since=300s` to confirm issues are actively happening now.
81: - `--timestamps` on log output helps correlate events across services.
82: - Check `Last State` timestamps in `describe pod` to see when the most recent crash actually occurred.
83: 
84: ### Cascade Detection
85: 
86: When many pods restart around the same time, check for a shared-dependency failure before investigating individual pods. The most common cascade: Redis goes down -> every service gets `ConnectionError`/`ConnectionRefusedError` -> mass restarts. Look for the same error across multiple `--previous` logs -- if they all say `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError`, debug Redis, not the individual services.
87: 
88: ## Log Analysis
89: 
90: ```bash
91: # All replicas of a service at once
92: kubectl logs -n crs -l app=fuzzer-bot --tail=100 --prefix
93: 
94: # Stream live
95: kubectl logs -n crs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=redis -f
96: 
97: # Collect all logs to disk (existing script)
98: bash deployment/collect-logs.sh
99: ```
100: 
101: ## Resource Pressure
102: 
103: ```bash
104: # Per-pod CPU/memory
105: kubectl top pods -n crs
106: 
107: # Node-level
108: kubectl top nodes
109: 
110: # Node conditions (disk pressure, memory pressure, PID pressure)
111: kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A5 Conditions
112: 
113: # Disk usage inside a pod
114: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- df -h
115: 
116: # What's eating disk
117: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- sh -c 'du -sh /corpus/* 2>/dev/null'
118: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- sh -c 'du -sh /scratch/* 2>/dev/null'
119: ```
120: 
121: ## Redis Debugging
122: 
123: Redis is the backbone. When it goes down, everything cascades.
124: 
125: ```bash
126: # Redis pod status
127: kubectl get pods -n crs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=redis
128: 
129: # Redis logs (AOF warnings, OOM, connection issues)
130: kubectl logs -n crs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=redis --tail=200
131: 
132: # Connect to Redis CLI
133: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli
134: 
135: # Inside redis-cli: key diagnostics
136: INFO memory          # used_memory_human, maxmemory
137: INFO persistence     # aof_enabled, aof_last_bgrewrite_status, aof_delayed_fsync
138: INFO clients         # connected_clients, blocked_clients
139: INFO stats           # total_connections_received, rejected_connections
140: CLIENT LIST          # see who's connected
141: DBSIZE               # total keys
142: 
143: # AOF configuration
144: CONFIG GET appendonly     # is AOF enabled?
145: CONFIG GET appendfsync   # fsync policy: everysec, always, or no
146: 
147: # What is /data mounted on? (disk vs tmpfs matters for AOF performance)
148: ```
149: 
150: ```bash
151: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- mount | grep /data
152: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- du -sh /data/
153: ```
154: 
155: ### Queue Inspection
156: 
157: Buttercup uses Redis streams with consumer groups. Queue names:
158: 
159: | Queue | Stream Key |
160: |-------|-----------|
161: | Build | fuzzer_build_queue |
162: | Build Output | fuzzer_build_output_queue |
163: | Crash | fuzzer_crash_queue |
164: | Confirmed Vulns | confirmed_vulnerabilities_queue |
165: | Download Tasks | orchestrator_download_tasks_queue |
166: | Ready Tasks | tasks_ready_queue |
167: | Patches | patches_queue |
168: | Index | index_queue |
169: | Index Output | index_output_queue |
170: | Traced Vulns | traced_vulnerabilities_queue |
171: | POV Requests | pov_reproducer_requests_queue |
172: | POV Responses | pov_reproducer_responses_queue |
173: | Delete Task | orchestrator_delete_task_queue |
174: 
175: ```bash
176: # Check stream length (pending messages)
177: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli XLEN fuzzer_build_queue
178: 
179: # Check consumer group lag
180: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli XINFO GROUPS fuzzer_build_queue
181: 
182: # Check pending messages per consumer
183: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli XPENDING fuzzer_build_queue build_bot_consumers - + 10
184: 
185: # Task registry size
186: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli HLEN tasks_registry
187: 
188: # Task state counts
189: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli SCARD cancelled_tasks
190: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli SCARD succeeded_tasks
191: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli SCARD errored_tasks
192: ```
193: 
194: Consumer groups: `build_bot_consumers`, `orchestrator_group`, `patcher_group`, `index_group`, `tracer_bot_group`.
195: 
196: ## Health Checks
197: 
198: Pods write timestamps to `/tmp/health_check_alive`. The liveness probe checks file freshness.
199: 
200: ```bash
201: # Check health file freshness
202: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- stat /tmp/health_check_alive
203: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- cat /tmp/health_check_alive
204: ```
205: 
206: If a pod is restart-looping, the health check file is likely going stale because the main process is blocked (e.g. waiting on Redis, stuck on I/O).
207: 
208: ## Telemetry (OpenTelemetry / Signoz)
209: 
210: All services export traces and metrics via OpenTelemetry. If Signoz is deployed (`global.signoz.deployed: true`), use its UI for distributed tracing across services.
211: 
212: ```bash
213: # Check if OTEL is configured
214: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- env | grep OTEL
215: 
216: # Verify Signoz pods are running (if deployed)
217: kubectl get pods -n platform -l app.kubernetes.io/name=signoz
218: ```
219: 
220: Traces are especially useful for diagnosing slow task processing, identifying which service in a pipeline is the bottleneck, and correlating events across the scheduler -> build-bot -> fuzzer-bot chain.
221: 
222: ## Volume and Storage
223: 
224: ```bash
225: # PVC status
226: kubectl get pvc -n crs
227: 
228: # Check if corpus tmpfs is mounted, its size, and backing type
229: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- mount | grep corpus_tmpfs
230: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- df -h /corpus_tmpfs 2>/dev/null
231: 
232: # Check if CORPUS_TMPFS_PATH is set
233: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- env | grep CORPUS
234: 
235: # Full disk layout - what's on real disk vs tmpfs
236: kubectl exec -n crs <pod> -- df -h
237: ```
238: 
239: `CORPUS_TMPFS_PATH` is set when `global.volumes.corpusTmpfs.enabled: true`. This affects fuzzer-bot, coverage-bot, seed-gen, and merger-bot.
240: 
241: ### Deployment Config Verification
242: 
243: When behavior doesn't match expectations, verify Helm values actually took effect:
244: 
245: ```bash
246: # Check a pod's actual resource limits
247: kubectl get pod -n crs <pod-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
248: 
249: # Check a pod's actual volume definitions
250: kubectl get pod -n crs <pod-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes}'
251: ```
252: 
253: Helm values template typos (e.g. wrong key names) silently fall back to chart defaults. If deployed resources don't match the values template, check for key name mismatches.
254: 
255: ## Service-Specific Debugging
256: 
257: For detailed per-service symptoms, root causes, and fixes, see [references/failure-patterns.md](references/failure-patterns.md).
258: 
259: Quick reference:
260: 
261: - **DinD**: `kubectl logs -n crs -l app=dind --tail=100` -- look for docker daemon crashes, storage driver errors
262: - **Build-bot**: check build queue depth, DinD connectivity, OOM during compilation
263: - **Fuzzer-bot**: corpus disk usage, CPU throttling, crash queue backlog
264: - **Patcher**: LiteLLM connectivity, LLM timeout, patch queue depth
265: - **Scheduler**: the central brain -- `kubectl logs -n crs -l app=scheduler --tail=-1 --prefix | grep "WAIT_PATCH_PASS\|ERROR\|SUBMIT"`
266: 
267: ## Diagnostic Script
268: 
269: Run the automated triage snapshot:
270: 
271: ```bash
272: bash {baseDir}/scripts/diagnose.sh
273: ```
274: 
275: Pass `--full` to also dump recent logs from all pods:
276: 
277: ```bash
278: bash {baseDir}/scripts/diagnose.sh --full
279: ```
280:

2: 
3: ## Table of Contents
4: 
5: 1. [Redis AOF Cascade](#redis-aof-cascade)
6: 2. [Disk Saturation from Corpus Writes](#disk-saturation-from-corpus-writes)
7: 3. [DinD Failures](#dind-failures)
8: 4. [OOM Kills](#oom-kills)
9: 5. [Queue Backlog Stalls](#queue-backlog-stalls)
10: 6. [Health Check Staleness](#health-check-staleness)

12: 
13: ---
14: 
15: ## Redis AOF Cascade
16: 
17: **Symptoms**: Multiple pods restart within minutes of each other. Redis logs show:
18: ```
19: Asynchronous AOF fsync is taking too long (disk is busy?)
20: ```
21: Services crash with `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Connection refused` or `Connection reset by peer`.
22: 
23: **Root cause**: Disk I/O contention blocks Redis `fsync()`. Even tiny AOF writes stall when the underlying disk is busy with other workloads (DinD, fuzzer corpus, etc.). Liveness probe fails. Redis restarts. All services lose connection and cascade-restart.
24: 
25: **Diagnosis**:
26: ```bash
27: # Check AOF delayed fsync count and config
28: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli INFO persistence | grep aof_delayed_fsync
29: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli CONFIG GET appendonly
30: # Check what /data is mounted on - disk vs tmpfs
31: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- mount | grep /data
32: # Confirm cascade: check if multiple pods crashed with the same Redis error
33: kubectl logs -n crs <other-pod> --previous --tail=20
34: ```
35: 
36: **Fixes**:
37: - Use memory-backed volume for Redis: `redis.master.persistence.medium: "Memory"` - AOF writes go to tmpfs, immune to disk contention
38: - Reduce disk I/O from other sources (corpus tmpfs, DinD storage)
39: - Note: `persistence.enabled` controls PVC creation, not AOF. AOF is set in Redis server config separately
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## Disk Saturation from Corpus Writes
44: 
45: **Symptoms**: Pods slow down or hang. `df -h` shows root filesystem nearly full. Node shows `DiskPressure` condition.
46: 
47: **Diagnosis**:
48: ```bash
49: kubectl describe node <node> | grep DiskPressure
50: kubectl exec -n crs <fuzzer-pod> -- du -sh /corpus/*
51: kubectl exec -n crs <fuzzer-pod> -- df -h
52: ```
53: 
54: **Fixes**:
55: - Enable corpus tmpfs (moves corpus to `/dev/shm`)
56: - Reduce fuzzer-bot replicas
57: - Enable scratch-cleaner with shorter retention (`scratchRetentionSeconds`)
58: - Increase node disk size
59: 
60: ---
61: 
62: ## DinD Failures
63: 
64: **Symptoms**: Build-bot jobs fail with `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon`. DinD pod restarting or in CrashLoopBackOff.
65: 
66: **Diagnosis**:
67: ```bash
68: kubectl logs -n crs -l app=dind --tail=100
69: kubectl describe pod -n crs <dind-pod>
70: kubectl exec -n crs <dind-pod> -- docker info
71: ```
72: 
73: **Common causes**:
74: - Storage driver errors (overlay2 on incompatible filesystem)
75: - DinD running out of disk space (images accumulating)
76: - Resource limits too low (DinD needs significant CPU/memory for builds)
77: 
78: **Fixes**:
79: - Increase DinD resource limits (8000m CPU, 16Gi memory for large deployments)
80: - Prune images periodically: `docker system prune -af`
81: - Check storage driver compatibility
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## OOM Kills
86: 
87: **Symptoms**: Pod status shows `OOMKilled`. Describe shows `Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled`.
88: 
89: **Diagnosis**:
90: ```bash
91: kubectl describe pod -n crs <pod> | grep -A3 "Last State"
92: kubectl get events -n crs | grep OOM
93: kubectl top pods -n crs --sort-by=memory
94: ```
95: 
96: **Common causes**:
97: - coverage-bot: needs 8Gi+ for large targets
98: - dind: building large projects
99: 
100: **Fixes**: Increase memory limits in values template for the affected service.
101: 
102: ---
103: 
104: ## Queue Backlog Stalls
105: 
106: **Symptoms**: Tasks not progressing. Scheduler logs show state stuck (e.g. never reaching `SUBMIT_BUNDLE`). Queue depths growing.
107: 
108: **Diagnosis**:
109: ```bash
110: # Check all queue depths
111: for q in fuzzer_build_queue fuzzer_build_output_queue fuzzer_crash_queue \
112:          confirmed_vulnerabilities_queue orchestrator_download_tasks_queue \
113:          orchestrator_delete_task_queue tasks_ready_queue patches_queue \
114:          index_queue index_output_queue traced_vulnerabilities_queue \
115:          pov_reproducer_requests_queue pov_reproducer_responses_queue; do
116:   echo "$q: $(kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli XLEN $q)"
117: done
118: 
119: # Check for stuck consumers
120: kubectl exec -n crs <redis-pod> -- redis-cli XINFO GROUPS fuzzer_build_queue
121: ```
122: 
123: **Common causes**:
124: - Consumer pod crashed and didn't ack messages - messages stuck in PEL (pending entries list)
125: - Downstream service down (e.g. build-bot down -> build queue grows)
126: - Task timeout too short (`BUILD_TASK_TIMEOUT_MS` default 15min)
127: 
128: **Fixes**:
129: - Restart the stuck consumer pods
130: - Claim and ack orphaned pending messages
131: - Increase task timeouts if builds are legitimately slow
132: 
133: ---
134: 
135: ## Health Check Staleness
136: 
137: **Symptoms**: Pod keeps restarting despite logs showing it was working. Describe shows `Liveness probe failed`.
138: 
139: **Root cause**: The main process is alive but blocked (e.g. waiting on Redis, slow I/O), so it doesn't update `/tmp/health_check_alive`. After 600s stale + probe timing, Kubernetes kills it.
140: 
141: **Diagnosis**:
142: ```bash
143: kubectl describe pod -n crs <pod> | grep -A5 "Liveness"
144: kubectl logs -n crs <pod> --previous --tail=50
145: ```
146: 
147: **Fixes**:
148: - Fix the underlying block (Redis connection, disk I/O)
149: - Increase `livenessProbe.periodSeconds` or `failureThreshold`
150: 
151: ---
152: 
153: ## Init Container Stuck on Redis
154: 
155: **Symptoms**: Pod stuck in `Init:0/1`. Events show init container running but never completing.
156: 
157: **Root cause**: The `wait-for-redis` init container polls `redis-master:6379`. If Redis is down, all pods queue up waiting.
158: 
159: **Diagnosis**:
160: ```bash
161: kubectl describe pod -n crs <pod> | grep -A10 "Init Containers"
162: kubectl get pods -n crs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=redis
163: ```
164: 
165: **Fix**: Fix Redis first. Everything else will unblock automatically.", "scripts/diagnose.sh": "1: #!/usr/bin/env bash
2: # Buttercup CRS diagnostic snapshot
3: # Collects pod status, events, resource usage, Redis health, and queue depths.
4: # Usage: bash diagnose.sh [--full]
5: #   --full: also dump recent logs from all pods (verbose)
6: 
7: set -euo pipefail
8: 
9: command -v kubectl >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
10:   echo "Error: kubectl not found"
11:   exit 1
12: }
13: 
14: NS="${BUTTERCUP_NAMESPACE:-crs}"
15: FULL=false
16: [[ "${1:-}" == "--full" ]] && FULL=true
17: 
18: section() { echo -e "\n===== $1 ====="; }
19: 
20: section "Pod Status"
21: kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -o wide
22: 
23: section "Pods with Restarts (termination reasons)"
24: for pod in $(kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount > 0)]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' 2>/dev/null); do
25:   restarts=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$pod" -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}' 2>/dev/null)
26:   reason=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$pod" -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}' 2>/dev/null)
27:   finished=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$pod" -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.finishedAt}' 2>/dev/null)
28:   printf "  %-55s restarts=%-3s reason=%-12s last=%s\n" "$pod" "$restarts" "${reason:--}" "${finished:--}"
29: done
30: 
31: section "Recent Warning Events"
32: kubectl get events -n "$NS" --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' 2>/dev/null | tail -30
33: 
34: section "Resource Usage (pods)"
35: kubectl top pods -n "$NS" 2>/dev/null || echo "(metrics-server not available)"
36: 
37: section "Resource Usage (nodes)"
38: kubectl top nodes 2>/dev/null || echo "(metrics-server not available)"
39: 
40: section "PVC Status"
41: kubectl get pvc -n "$NS" 2>/dev/null || echo "(no PVCs)"
42: 
43: # Find a redis pod
44: REDIS_POD=$(kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -l app.kubernetes.io/name=redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}' 2>/dev/null || true)
45: 
46: if [[ -n "$REDIS_POD" ]]; then
